items.answer: The first Five-Year Plan began

items.stem: Source D is a statement by President Carter, January 1980 (summary). Carter called the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan the greatest threat to peace since the Second World War and announced sanctions and the withdrawal of SALT II from the Senate. Study the source. Which statement best describes the message of Source D?
options: It suggests the invasion achieved military control but not popular support.
It shows Gorbachev rejecting the use of force and the Brezhnev Doctrine.
It suggests the blockade led the West to seek a formal alliance.
It shows Carter abandoning détente because of Afghanistan.
items.answer: It shows Carter abandoning détente because of Afghanistan.
items.markingKey: Only this statement matches the content of Source D. [1]

items.stem: Kwame ends an essay on “‘Reagan restored the power and prestige of the presidency.’ How far do you agree?” with this conclusion: “Reagan restored confidence in the presidency after the 1970s, though Iran-Contra showed the risks of its power.” Explain one piece of evidence that supports this conclusion and one point a critic could make against it.
items.answer: Evidence the conclusion rests on (either strand of the judgement), for example: He won landslides in 1980 and 1984. / Iran-Contra showed abuse of power. Possible criticism: the conclusion may underplay the point that his communication skills restored public confidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for relevant supporting evidence and 1 mark for explaining how it supports the judgement; 1 mark for a valid counter-point and 1 mark for developing it [3]

items.stem: Consider the following explanations of why orthodox historians blamed the Soviet Union for the Cold War. A: They had access mainly to Western sources. B: Events such as the Czech coup and the Berlin Blockade looked like aggression. C: Soviet control of Eastern Europe broke the promises of Yalta. Explain how these reasons were linked and decide which mattered most.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: They had access mainly to Western sources. B: Events such as the Czech coup and the Berlin Blockade looked like aggression. C: Soviet control of Eastern Europe broke the promises of Yalta. Possible judgement: Soviet actions in Eastern Europe, interpreted through the climate of the early Cold War, made Soviet responsibility seem obvious.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [5]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Income inequality grew in the 1980s.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Accurate. Gains went disproportionately to the highest earners.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [1]

items.stem: ‘Cold War pressures were the main obstacle to nation-building in Southeast Asia after independence.’ How far do you agree with this view?
items.answer: For: War in Vietnam and Indochina. Communist insurgencies and US intervention. Superpower support for military regimes. Against: Ethnic divisions in Malaysia, Burma and elsewhere. Economic weakness and poverty. Authoritarian leaders such as Sukarno, Ne Win and Marcos. Judgement: Cold War pressures were decisive in Indochina, but elsewhere internal divisions and authoritarian rule were the main obstacles.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): a focused, balanced and analytical answer with a sustained, well-supported judgement; precise and relevant knowledge throughout. Level 4 (13-16): analysis of both sides with a judgement, though not fully sustained or supported. Level 3 (9-12): some analysis, but one-sided or uneven, or with descriptive passages. Level 2 (5-8): mainly descriptive or narrative, with limited links to the question. Level 1 (1-4): general, unsupported or irrelevant points. (The examination essay is marked out of 30; levels are scaled.) Agree / supporting: War in Vietnam and Indochina. Communist insurgencies and US intervention. Superpower support for military regimes. Disagree / other factors: Ethnic divisions in Malaysia, Burma and elsewhere. Economic weakness and poverty. Authoritarian leaders such as Sukarno, Ne Win and Marcos. Possible judgement: Cold War pressures were decisive in Indochina, but elsewhere internal divisions and authoritarian rule were the main obstacles. [19]

items.stem: Study Source C. Source C: a newspaper report, Berlin, March 1933 (illustrative). “The deputies made their way to the Kroll Opera House through lines of SA men chanting "We want the bill - or fire and murder!"” How reliable is Source C as evidence about the passing of the Enabling Act? Use the provenance of the source and your own knowledge.
items.answer: Reliable because it is a contemporary report. Less reliable because the press was already under pressure in March 1933. Cross-reference: It does not show how deputies voted or why. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view, but it needs to be tested against other evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point about the content; up to 2 marks for using the provenance (author, date, purpose, audience) to judge reliability; up to 2 marks for cross-referencing with own knowledge; 1 mark for a supported overall judgement [5]

items.stem: Study the extract. “In the occupied east in the summer of 1941 the killing spread from Jewish men of military age to women and children. The decisive steps were often taken by commanders on the spot, competing to show their zeal and reporting their "successes" to Berlin. Policy was made as much in the occupied cities of the east as in the Reich Chancellery.” (A historian writing in 1999 (illustrative).) What can you learn from this extract about the interpretation and approach of the historian who wrote it? Use the extract and your knowledge of the Holocaust to explain your answer.
items.answer: Interpretation: Radicalisation came from initiatives in the occupied territories as much as from orders from the centre. Approach: The historian focuses on local initiatives in the occupied territories, using regional records. Own knowledge that supports it: Einsatzgruppen reports show competition in numbers killed. Killing of women and children spread from late July and August 1941. Babi Yar, September 1941, was organised locally with the army. Own knowledge that challenges it: Himmler toured the east and encouraged escalation. The killing was consistent with Hitler's ideological war. Central decisions were needed for deportations from the Reich.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): demonstrates a full understanding of the historian's interpretation and approach, explained with close reference to the extract and tested against accurate own knowledge. Level 4 (13-16): explains the main interpretation with support from the extract and shows some understanding of the approach. Level 3 (9-12): identifies the main interpretation with some support, or explains sub-messages. Level 2 (5-8): identifies sub-messages or makes valid points about the topic linked to the extract. Level 1 (1-4): paraphrases or summarises the extract, or writes about the topic without reference to it. (The examination question is marked out of 40; levels are scaled.) [19]

items.stem: Source A is a newspaper editorial, 1967 (illustrative). “The slogan of Black Power has frightened the very people whose votes passed the Civil Rights Act. Every riot makes the next law harder to pass.” Study the source. What can you learn from Source A about reactions to Black Power? Support your answer with details from the source.
items.answer: It suggests Black Power and riots caused a white backlash. Supporting details: for example, “The slogan of Black Power has frightened the very people whose votes passed the Civil Rights Act”; each detail should be linked to an inference.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each valid inference and 1 mark for each supporting detail from the source [3]

items.stem: Read the sources carefully. Source A: a report by a British diplomat in Rome, 1932 (illustrative). “Wages have been cut repeatedly and the high lira has hit the export trades. The regime speaks of corporations, but in practice the employers decide.” Source B: a Fascist propaganda poster for the Battle for Grain, 1920s (description). The poster shows Mussolini, stripped to the waist, threshing wheat beside peasant farmers under a bright sun. How far do Sources A and B support the view that Fascist economic policies were a failure?
items.answer: Source A supports: it shows economic policy harming workers and exports. Evaluation: a foreign observer might lack contact with ordinary Italians. Source B challenges: it presents economic policy as a success. Evaluation: it is propaganda and tells us nothing about real results. Grouping: support A; challenge B. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): evaluates the sources (provenance, purpose, context, cross-reference) to show how far they support AND challenge the view, reaching a supported judgement. Level 4 (13-16): uses the sources to support AND challenge the view and evaluates some of them. Level 3 (9-12): uses the sources at face value to support AND challenge. Level 2 (5-8): uses the sources to support OR challenge. Level 1 (1-4): writes about the topic without valid use of the sources. (The examination version uses four sources and 25 marks; levels are scaled.) [19]

items.stem: Study the extract. “Neither side sought a Cold War. Each acted to secure itself, and each read the other's defensive moves as offensive. items.stem: Consider the following explanations of why historians have increasingly stressed shared responsibility for the war. A: The Fischer thesis was criticised for reading German aims backwards from 1914. B: The end of the Cold War reduced the political weight of the German guilt debate. C: Research in Austrian, Russian, Serbian and French archives revealed their leaders' choices. Which was the most significant? Explain your answer with reference to the other reasons.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: The Fischer thesis was criticised for reading German aims backwards from 1914. B: The end of the Cold War reduced the political weight of the German guilt debate. C: Research in Austrian, Russian, Serbian and French archives revealed their leaders' choices. Possible judgement: new archival evidence from other capitals widened the focus beyond Berlin.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: Sofia ends an essay on “How far was the formation of the Warsaw Pact a response to Western actions?” with this conclusion: “It was triggered by West German rearmament, but it mainly formalised Soviet control that already existed.” Explain one piece of evidence that supports this conclusion and one point a critic could make against it.
items.answer: Evidence the conclusion rests on (either strand of the judgement), for example: It followed West Germany's entry into NATO within days. / Soviet control of Eastern Europe already existed through bilateral treaties. Possible criticism: the conclusion may underplay the point that it mirrored NATO.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for relevant supporting evidence and 1 mark for explaining how it supports the judgement; 1 mark for a valid counter-point and 1 mark for developing it [4]

items.stem: Study Sources A and C. Source A: Richard Nixon, press conference, November 1973 (abridged). “People have got to know whether or not their President is a crook. Well, I'm not a crook.” Source C: a newspaper editorial, August 1974 (illustrative). “The system has worked. A free press, an independent judiciary and a Congress that did its duty have shown that no man, not even a President, is above the law.” Compare and contrast the views of Sources A and C on Watergate and the presidency.
items.answer: Source A: Nixon publicly denies wrongdoing. Source C: It suggests Watergate showed the strength of the constitution rather than its weakness. They should be compared on what each says about Watergate and the presidency; similarities and differences should be supported with details. Provenance: A is Richard Nixon, press conference, November 1973 (abridged) (the tapes later showed he had approved the cover-up); C is a newspaper editorial, August 1974 (illustrative) (it is an opinion written in the moment). Differences in authorship, date and purpose explain the contrast.
items.markingKey: Level 4 (12-15): compares and contrasts the sources, explaining similarities AND differences, and evaluates them using provenance and context to explain why they differ. Level 3 (8-11): explains similarities AND differences in content, supported by details from both sources. Level 2 (4-7): explains a similarity OR a difference. Level 1 (1-3): describes or paraphrases the content of the sources without valid comparison. [15]

items.stem: Study Source B. Source B: the Port Huron Statement, 1962 (abridged). “We are people of this generation, bred in at least modest comfort, housed now in universities, looking uncomfortably to the world we inherit.” Assess the reliability of Source B as evidence about student radicalism.
items.answer: Reliable because it is the founding statement of the main New Left group. Less reliable because it represents a small group of student activists. items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point about the content; up to 2 marks for using the provenance (author, date, purpose, audience) to judge reliability; up to 2 marks for cross-referencing with own knowledge; 1 mark for a supported overall judgement [6]

items.stem: By 1941 every country in Southeast Asia except Siam (Thailand) was under colonial rule. ‘Nationalist movements in Southeast Asia were weak before 1941.’ How far do you agree with this view?
items.answer: For: Colonial repression in Indonesia and Vietnam. Ethnic divisions in Malaya. Limited mass support outside the elites. Against: Sarekat Islam had mass membership. The Youth Pledge created a sense of Indonesian identity. The Philippines won a promise of independence. Judgement: nationalism had developed ideas and leaders by 1941, but colonial power prevented it from achieving independence.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): a focused, balanced and analytical answer with a sustained, well-supported judgement; precise and relevant knowledge throughout. Level 4 (13-16): analysis of both sides with a judgement, though not fully sustained or supported. Level 3 (9-12): some analysis, but one-sided or uneven, or with descriptive passages. Level 2 (5-8): mainly descriptive or narrative, with limited links to the question. Level 1 (1-4): general, unsupported or irrelevant points. (The examination essay is marked out of 30; levels are scaled.) Agree / supporting: Colonial repression in Indonesia and Vietnam. Ethnic divisions in Malaya. Limited mass support outside the elites. Disagree / other factors: Sarekat Islam had mass membership. The Youth Pledge created a sense of Indonesian identity. The Philippines won a promise of independence. Possible judgement: nationalism had developed ideas and leaders by 1941, but colonial power prevented it from achieving independence. [20]

items.stem: Study Source C. items.answer: Challenges: it suggests the support of elites, not the crisis itself, was decisive However, it is a private view, perhaps written in despair.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid judgement; up to 2 marks for details of the source used to support it; up to 2 marks for evaluating the source (provenance or own knowledge) [5]

items.stem: Study Sources B and C. Source B: Jimmy Carter, televised address, July 1979 (summary). Carter spoke of a "crisis of confidence" among Americans and called on them to save energy and work together to overcome the nation's problems. Source C: a newspaper report from a petrol station, 1974 (illustrative). “The queue stretched for half a mile. Drivers who had waited two hours were told the pumps were dry. Prices have doubled since the autumn.” Compare and contrast Sources B and C as evidence about the US economy in the 1970s.
items.answer: Source B: It shows the president presenting the crisis as one of national morale. Source C: It shows shortages and rising prices caused by the oil crisis. They should be compared on what each says about the US economy in the 1970s; similarities and differences should be supported with details. Provenance: B is Jimmy Carter, televised address, July 1979 (summary) (it was a political speech that many saw as blaming the public); C is a newspaper report from a petrol station, 1974 (illustrative) (it describes one place and day). Differences in authorship, date and purpose explain the contrast.
items.markingKey: Level 4 (12-15): compares and contrasts the sources, explaining similarities AND differences, and evaluates them using provenance and context to explain why they differ. Level 3 (8-11): explains similarities AND differences in content, supported by details from both sources. Level 2 (4-7): explains a similarity OR a difference. items.stem: Study Sources C and D. Source C: a letter from a worker in Magnitogorsk, 1932 (illustrative). “We live in tents and barracks, and there is never enough bread. But the blast furnaces are rising, and they say that soon we will make more steel than all of England.” Source D: Stalin, speech to industrial managers, February 1931 (translated, abridged). “We are fifty or a hundred years behind the advanced countries. We must make good this distance in ten years. Either we do it, or they crush us.” Compare and contrast the views of Sources C and D on the Great Turn.
items.answer: Source C: It suggests that industrial growth was rapid but living conditions were very hard. Source D: Stalin argues that rapid industrialisation is necessary to survive attack by the capitalist powers. They should be compared on what each says about the Great Turn; similarities and differences should be supported with details. Provenance: C is a letter from a worker in Magnitogorsk, 1932 (illustrative) (letters were often censored, so he may have been cautious); D is Stalin, speech to industrial managers, February 1931 (translated, abridged) (it is a speech intended to drive managers harder). Differences in authorship, date and purpose explain the contrast.
items.markingKey: Level 4 (12-15): compares and contrasts the sources, explaining similarities AND differences, and evaluates them using provenance and context to explain why they differ. items.stem: Read the extract and then answer the question. Extract: a historian writing in the 1960s (illustrative). “The war of 1914 was a war for the redivision of the world. Finance capital in Britain, Germany and France had outgrown its national markets; colonies, spheres of investment and sources of raw materials were the stakes. Governments managed this competition, and the workers of every nation were sent to die for it.” How far does your own knowledge support the interpretation in the extract? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Supporting evidence: Imperial rivalry in Africa and the Moroccan crises. Anglo-German trade competition. The Berlin-Baghdad railway alarmed Britain and Russia. Challenging evidence: Britain and Germany were major trading partners and many bankers opposed war. The crisis began in the Balkans, not over colonies. Imperial disputes such as Fashoda were settled peacefully. Judgement: the interpretation is supported in part; its strength depends on the evidence it emphasises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the interpretation; up to 4 marks for own knowledge that supports it and up to 4 for knowledge that challenges it, each linked to the extract; 1 mark for a supported judgement [9]

items.stem: Historians' interpretations of the Holocaust have changed as new evidence has become available, including Eastern European archives after 1991. ‘Hitler's role was the decisive factor in the Holocaust.’ How far do you agree with this view?
items.answer: For: His ideology defined the Jews as the enemy. His approval was needed for key decisions. His prophecy and speeches set the direction. Against: Rival agencies radicalised policy. Local initiatives drove killing. Ordinary perpetrators, collaborators and bystanders made it possible. Judgement: Hitler's role was necessary but not sufficient: the Holocaust required a system and many participants to carry it out.

Level 2 (5-8): mainly descriptive or narrative, with limited links to the question. Level 1 (1-4): general, unsupported or irrelevant points. (The examination essay is marked out of 30; levels are scaled.) Agree / supporting: His ideology defined the Jews as the enemy. His approval was needed for key decisions. His prophecy and speeches set the direction. Disagree / other factors: Rival agencies radicalised policy. Local initiatives drove killing. Ordinary perpetrators, collaborators and bystanders made it possible. Possible judgement: Hitler's role was necessary but not sufficient: the Holocaust required a system and many participants to carry it out. [19]

items.stem: How far was the Marshall Plan an act of economic imperialism?
items.answer: For: It opened European markets to US goods. It tied recipients to US economic policy. It aimed to prevent communist parties winning in Western Europe. Against: It was offered to all of Europe, including the USSR. It helped European recovery and was welcomed. European governments shaped how aid was used. Judgement: it served US economic and political interests, but it was also a genuine recovery programme that Europeans welcomed.

Level 4 (13-16): analysis of both sides with a judgement, though not fully sustained or supported. Level 3 (9-12): some analysis, but one-sided or uneven, or with descriptive passages. Level 2 (5-8): mainly descriptive or narrative, with limited links to the question. Level 1 (1-4): general, unsupported or irrelevant points. (The examination essay is marked out of 30; levels are scaled.) Agree / supporting: It opened European markets to US goods. It tied recipients to US economic policy. It aimed to prevent communist parties winning in Western Europe. Disagree / other factors: It was offered to all of Europe, including the USSR. It helped European recovery and was welcomed. European governments shaped how aid was used. Possible judgement: it served US economic and political interests, but it was also a genuine recovery programme that Europeans welcomed. [19]

items.stem: Study Source C. Source C: Mussolini, speech to the Chamber of Deputies, 3 January 1925 (translated, abridged). “I declare that I, and I alone, assume the political, moral and historical responsibility for all that has happened.” Assess the reliability of Source C as evidence about Mussolini's response to the Matteotti crisis.
items.answer: Reliable because it is Mussolini's own words at the turning point. Less reliable because it is a political performance designed to intimidate. Cross-reference: It does not show the role of the king or the opposition. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view, but it needs to be tested against other evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point about the content; up to 2 marks for using the provenance (author, date, purpose, audience) to judge reliability; up to 2 marks for cross-referencing with own knowledge; 1 mark for a supported overall judgement [5]

items.stem: Kenji ends an essay on “‘Germany was mainly responsible for the outbreak of war in 1914.’ How far do you agree?” with this conclusion: “Germany bears a heavy share of responsibility for turning a Balkan crisis into a European war, but it was not alone.” Explain one piece of evidence that supports this conclusion and one point a critic could make against it.
items.answer: Evidence the conclusion rests on (either strand of the judgement), for example: The blank cheque encouraged Austria to take a hard line. / Austria-Hungary decided on war against Serbia for its own reasons. Possible criticism: the conclusion may underplay the point that German leaders believed a war sooner was better than later.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for relevant supporting evidence and 1 mark for explaining how it supports the judgement; 1 mark for a valid counter-point and 1 mark for developing it [3]

items.stem: Read the two extracts. Extract A: a historian writing in the 1970s (illustrative). “In March 1947 the President told Congress that the world faced a choice between two ways of life. The danger in Greece and Turkey did not justify such language; it was chosen to frighten a reluctant Congress into paying. The Truman Doctrine turned a local crisis into a global crusade.” Extract B: a historian writing in the late 1950s (illustrative). “American leaders believed that the prosperity of the United States depended on an open world economy. The Open Door, not the Iron Curtain, was the starting point of their policy. The Marshall Plan offered aid on terms that would tie Europe to American markets, and Moscow could hardly be expected to accept them.” Which extract offers the more convincing interpretation of the origins of the Cold War? Use both extracts and your own knowledge to explain your answer.
items.answer: Extract A: The Truman Doctrine deliberately exaggerated the Soviet threat, turning local crises into a global confrontation. Support: Britain's withdrawal from Greece created the immediate need for aid. Challenge: Soviet pressure on Turkey over the Straits was real. Extract B: US economic expansion and the pursuit of an open world economy caused the Cold War. Support: The USA sought free trade through Bretton Woods. Challenge: Soviet control of Eastern Europe preceded the Marshall Plan. Any supported judgement.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): evaluates both interpretations against own knowledge and their approach and use of evidence, reaching a sustained judgement on which is more convincing. Level 4 (13-16): tests both interpretations against own knowledge with a judgement. Level 3 (9-12): explains both interpretations and tests one. Level 2 (5-8): explains the interpretations without testing them. Level 1 (1-4): paraphrases the extracts. [19]

items.stem: Read the extract and then answer the question. Extract: a historian writing in 1992 (illustrative). “The men of the battalion were middle-aged reservists from a German city, not committed Nazis. When offered the chance to step out before their first massacre, only a handful did. Most killed because they did not want to break ranks, to appear weak, or to leave the dirty work to their comrades.” Explain how the time and circumstances in which the historian was writing might have shaped this interpretation.
items.answer: This reflects the approach of Christopher Browning's Ordinary Men (1992), which used the interrogations of members of Reserve Police Battalion 101. This helps explain the interpretation: Ordinary men became killers mainly because of conformity, peer pressure and wartime circumstances rather than ideology.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant context; up to 2 marks for explaining it; up to 2 marks for linking it to features of the interpretation in the extract [4]

items.stem: Study all the sources. Source A: a historian writing in 1990 (illustrative). “The war accelerated movements whose roots lay in the 1920s. Without the nationalist parties built before 1941, there would have been no leaders ready to seize the moment in 1945.” Source B: a Burmese nationalist memoir, written in the 1950s (illustrative). “When the British ran from Rangoon, the spell was broken. The Japanese gave us arms and titles, but not freedom; so in 1945 we turned the guns on them.” “The Japanese occupation was the main reason for the growth of nationalism in Southeast Asia.” How far do Sources A and B support this view?
items.answer: Source A challenges: it stresses pre-war roots. Evaluation: it is one view. Source B supports: it shows the occupation strengthening nationalism. Evaluation: written later, it may justify cooperation with Japan. Grouping: support B; challenge A. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): evaluates the sources (provenance, purpose, context, cross-reference) to show how far they support AND challenge the view, reaching a supported judgement. Level 4 (13-16): uses the sources to support AND challenge the view and evaluates some of them. Level 3 (9-12): uses the sources at face value to support AND challenge. Level 2 (5-8): uses the sources to support OR challenge. Level 1 (1-4): writes about the topic without valid use of the sources. (The examination version uses four sources and 25 marks; levels are scaled.) [19]

items.stem: Study Source D. Source D: a newspaper report, Berlin, March 1933 (illustrative). “The deputies made their way to the Kroll Opera House through lines of SA men chanting "We want the bill - or fire and murder!"” What does Source D reveal about the passing of the Enabling Act? Use details of the source to support your answer.
items.answer: It suggests intimidation surrounded the vote. Supporting details: for example, “The deputies made their way to the Kroll Opera House through lines of SA men chanting "We want the bill - or fire and murder!"”; each detail should be linked to an inference.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each valid inference and 1 mark for each supporting detail from the source [3]

items.stem: ‘The rise of the New Right was mainly a reaction against the counterculture of the 1960s.’ How far do you agree with this view?
items.answer: For: Evangelicals opposed permissiveness, drugs and sexual liberation. Nixon appealed to the silent majority against protesters. Opposition to Roe v. Wade and the ERA. Against: Economic problems of the 1970s drove support for tax cuts. Opposition to busing and racial change. Foreign policy humiliations such as Vietnam and Iran. Judgement: reaction against the 1960s gave the New Right its moral energy, but economic discontent broadened its appeal.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): a focused, balanced and analytical answer with a sustained, well-supported judgement; precise and relevant knowledge throughout. Level 4 (13-16): analysis of both sides with a judgement, though not fully sustained or supported. Level 3 (9-12): some analysis, but one-sided or uneven, or with descriptive passages. Level 2 (5-8): mainly descriptive or narrative, with limited links to the question. Level 1 (1-4): general, unsupported or irrelevant points. (The examination essay is marked out of 30; levels are scaled.) Agree / supporting: Evangelicals opposed permissiveness, drugs and sexual liberation. Nixon appealed to the silent majority against protesters. Opposition to Roe v. Wade and the ERA. Disagree / other factors: Economic problems of the 1970s drove support for tax cuts. Opposition to busing and racial change. Foreign policy humiliations such as Vietnam and Iran. Possible judgement: reaction against the 1960s gave the New Right its moral energy, but economic discontent broadened its appeal. [20]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this description: “the walk-out of opposition deputies from parliament after the murder of Matteotti in 1924”.
items.answer: Aventine Secession
items.markingKey: Aventine Secession: the walk-out of opposition deputies from parliament after the murder of Matteotti in 1924. [1]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this description: “Nixon's measures of August 1971, including ending gold convertibility of the dollar and a wage-price freeze”.
items.answer: Nixon Shock
items.markingKey: Nixon Shock: Nixon's measures of August 1971, including ending gold convertibility of the dollar and a wage-price freeze. [1]

items.stem: Study the extract. “To ask whether Hitler planned the Holocaust is to ask the wrong question. The regime set itself an impossible aim, a Germany "free of Jews", and every failure to achieve it by deportation increased the pressure for more radical measures. The bureaucracy did not need orders; it needed only a goal.” (A historian writing in the 1980s (illustrative).) Which of these best describes the approach of the historian who wrote the extract?
options: Focus on the structures of the Nazi state and bureaucracy
Focus on the behaviour and motives of individual perpetrators
Focus on collaborators and bystanders across occupied Europe
Focus on Hitler's ideology and statements
items.answer: Focus on the structures of the Nazi state and bureaucracy
items.markingKey: The historian focuses on how the bureaucracy worked and how failure produced radicalisation, rather than on Hitler's decisions. [1]

items.stem: Source D is the Youth Pledge, October 1928 (translated). “We, the sons and daughters of Indonesia, declare that we belong to one motherland, Indonesia. We declare that we belong to one nation, the Indonesian nation. We uphold the language of unity, the Indonesian language.” Study the source. Which statement best describes the message of Source D?
options: The historian argues pre-war nationalism was essential.
Eisenhower argues that the fall of one country to communism would lead to others falling.
Ho uses the words of the American Declaration to claim the right to independence.
It shows young nationalists claiming a single Indonesian identity.
items.answer: It shows young nationalists claiming a single Indonesian identity.
items.markingKey: Only this statement matches the content of Source D. [1]

items.stem: Study the extract. “Within months of Yalta, the Soviet Union had broken its promise of free elections in Poland and was installing obedient communist governments across Eastern Europe. Stalin's ideology taught him that conflict with the capitalist world was inevitable, and he expanded wherever he met no resistance. The Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan were the West's belated response.” (A historian writing in the 1950s (illustrative).) Identify the historian's interpretation of the origins of the Cold War and explain how the extract supports it.
items.answer: Interpretation: Soviet expansionism, driven by Stalin and communist ideology, caused the Cold War, and the USA responded defensively. Support from the extract: for example, “Within months of Yalta, the Soviet Union had broken its promise of free elections in Poland and was installing obedient communist governments across Eastern Europe.”
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a sub-message; 2 marks for the main interpretation; up to 1 mark for supporting detail from the extract [2]

items.stem: Read Source C. The party warned that the white race faced being swamped by the Black majority and promised apartheid to keep the races separate and protect white jobs. (A National Party election statement, 1948 (summary).) How reliable is Source C as evidence about the 1948 election? Use the provenance of the source and your own knowledge.
items.answer: Reliable because it shows the party's own message. Less reliable because it is election propaganda. Cross-reference: It does not show Afrikaner cultural motives. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view, but it needs to be tested against other evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point about the content; up to 2 marks for using the provenance (author, date, purpose, audience) to judge reliability; up to 2 marks for cross-referencing with own knowledge; 1 mark for a supported overall judgement [5]

items.stem: Analyse the reasons why McCarthyism gained support in 1950-54.
items.answer: Fear after the Soviet atomic bomb and the fall of China in 1949. Spy cases such as Hiss and the Rosenbergs. The Korean War from 1950. Republicans used anti-communism against the Democrats. Truman's Loyalty Program had already legitimised loyalty checks. Judgement: international shocks created fear, which Republicans and McCarthy exploited for political advantage.
items.markingKey: Level 4 (9-10): analyses a range of factors, showing how they interact, with a supported judgement on their relative importance. Level 3 (6-8): explains two or more factors with accurate support. Level 2 (3-5): describes or identifies factors, or explains one. Level 1 (1-2): general points. Indicative content: Fear after the Soviet atomic bomb and the fall of China in 1949. Spy cases such as Hiss and the Rosenbergs. The Korean War from 1950. Republicans used anti-communism against the Democrats. Truman's Loyalty Program had already legitimised loyalty checks. Possible judgement: international shocks created fear, which Republicans and McCarthy exploited for political advantage. [9]

items.stem: Study Sources A and C. Source A: a report by an SPD underground observer (Sopade), 1936 (summary). The reports noted that many workers were glad to have jobs and enjoyed KdF trips, but grumbled about long hours, low wages and food prices. Source C: a Nazi poster advertising the KdF car, 1938 (description). The poster shows a family in a shiny Volkswagen on an autobahn, with the slogan "Save five marks a week if you want your own car!" Compare and contrast the views of Sources A and C on the Nazi economy and society.
items.answer: Source A: It suggests workers had mixed feelings: grateful for jobs but resentful of conditions. Source C: It promises workers a share in prosperity. They disagree about whether the Nazi regime created a genuine Volksgemeinschaft; similarities and differences should be supported with details. Provenance: A is a report by an SPD underground observer (Sopade), 1936 (summary) (observers were opponents of the regime and might emphasise discontent); C is a Nazi poster advertising the KdF car, 1938 (description) (it is propaganda; very few savers ever received a car). Differences in authorship, date and purpose explain the contrast.
items.markingKey: Level 4 (12-15): compares and contrasts the sources, explaining similarities AND differences, and evaluates them using provenance and context to explain why they differ. Level 3 (8-11): explains similarities AND differences in content, supported by details from both sources. Level 2 (4-7): explains a similarity OR a difference. Level 1 (1-3): describes or paraphrases the content of the sources without valid comparison. [14]

items.stem: Source D is a memo by a Soviet economist, 1986 (illustrative). “We cannot match the Americans in new weapons and feed our people at the same time. Oil revenue has collapsed. Without reductions in military spending the economy will not survive.” Study the source. How reliable is Source D as evidence about Soviet economic problems? Use the provenance of the source and your own knowledge.
items.answer: Reliable because it shows thinking inside the Soviet system. Less reliable because it is one adviser's view. Cross-reference: It does not show Gorbachev's ideas. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view, but it needs to be tested against other evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point about the content; up to 2 marks for using the provenance (author, date, purpose, audience) to judge reliability; up to 2 marks for cross-referencing with own knowledge; 1 mark for a supported overall judgement [5]

items.stem: Study the extract. “By 1914 the European states system had become rigid. Two armed blocs faced each other; mobilisation plans left statesmen almost no time to negotiate. Arms races and imperial rivalries had created a climate in which war was widely expected. The assassination at Sarajevo merely lit a fuse that had long been laid.” (A historian writing in the 1980s (illustrative).) What can you learn from this extract about the interpretation and approach of the historian who wrote it? Use the extract and your knowledge of the origins of the First World War to explain your answer.
items.answer: Interpretation: The war was caused by long-term forces, such as alliances, arms races and military planning, rather than by the decisions of one government. Approach: The historian stresses long-term impersonal forces and the international system rather than individual decisions. Own knowledge that supports it: The Triple Alliance and Triple Entente divided Europe. The Anglo-German naval race increased mistrust. The Schlieffen Plan required rapid mobilisation and an attack on France. Own knowledge that challenges it: Italy stayed neutral in 1914, so alliances were not automatic. Earlier crises such as Morocco and Bosnia were settled peacefully. Individual decisions in July 1914 were crucial.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): demonstrates a full understanding of the historian's interpretation and approach, explained with close reference to the extract and tested against accurate own knowledge. Level 4 (13-16): explains the main interpretation with support from the extract and shows some understanding of the approach. Level 3 (9-12): identifies the main interpretation with some support, or explains sub-messages. Level 2 (5-8): identifies sub-messages or makes valid points about the topic linked to the extract. Level 1 (1-4): paraphrases or summarises the extract, or writes about the topic without reference to it. (The examination question is marked out of 40; levels are scaled.) [20]

items.stem: Read Source A. “Dr King came for a day and the cameras came with him. When they left, it was local people who kept on, house by house, for years.” (A memoir by a SNCC voter-registration worker in Mississippi, 1970s (illustrative).) What does Source A reveal about grassroots activism? Use details of the source to support your answer.
items.answer: It suggests that local activists, not national leaders, did most of the work. Supporting details: for example, “Dr King came for a day and the cameras came with him”; each detail should be linked to an inference.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each valid inference and 1 mark for each supporting detail from the source [4]

items.stem: Study Sources A and C. Source A: a letter from a worker in Magnitogorsk, 1932 (illustrative). “We live in tents and barracks, and there is never enough bread. But the blast furnaces are rising, and they say that soon we will make more steel than all of England.” Source C: Stalin, speech to industrial managers, February 1931 (translated, abridged). “We are fifty or a hundred years behind the advanced countries. We must make good this distance in ten years. Either we do it, or they crush us.” Compare and contrast the views of Sources A and C on the Great Turn.
items.answer: Source A: It suggests that industrial growth was rapid but living conditions were very hard. Source C: Stalin argues that rapid industrialisation is necessary to survive attack by the capitalist powers. They should be compared on what each says about the Great Turn; similarities and differences should be supported with details. Provenance: A is a letter from a worker in Magnitogorsk, 1932 (illustrative) (letters were often censored, so he may have been cautious); C is Stalin, speech to industrial managers, February 1931 (translated, abridged) (it is a speech intended to drive managers harder). Differences in authorship, date and purpose explain the contrast.
items.markingKey: Level 4 (12-15): compares and contrasts the sources, explaining similarities AND differences, and evaluates them using provenance and context to explain why they differ. Level 3 (8-11): explains similarities AND differences in content, supported by details from both sources. Level 2 (4-7): explains a similarity OR a difference. Level 1 (1-3): describes or paraphrases the content of the sources without valid comparison. [15]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this description: “the Serbian nationalist secret society linked to the assassination of Franz Ferdinand”.
items.answer: Black Hand
items.markingKey: Black Hand: the Serbian nationalist secret society linked to the assassination of Franz Ferdinand. [1]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this description: “restructuring, Gorbachev's attempt to reform the Soviet economy”.
items.answer: Perestroika
items.markingKey: Perestroika: restructuring, Gorbachev's attempt to reform the Soviet economy. [1]

items.stem: Which of these events happened first?
options: Hitler made his Reichstag "prophecy" about the annihilation of the Jews
items.answer: Mein Kampf was first published
items.markingKey: Mein Kampf was first published (1925); the Nuremberg Laws were passed (September 1935); Kristallnacht took place (9 November 1938); Hitler made his Reichstag "prophecy" about the annihilation of the Jews (30 January 1939). [1]

items.stem: Read Source C carefully. “One hundred years ago our fathers went into the wilderness to be free. Today the volk must again unite to take its rightful place in its own land.” (A speech at the Great Trek centenary, 1938 (illustrative).) Which statement best describes the message of Source C?
options: It suggests Soweto marked a new phase of mass resistance.
It shows Botha accepting limited reform as necessary for survival.
It suggests economic pressure forced change.
It shows the strength of Afrikaner nationalist feeling.
items.answer: It shows the strength of Afrikaner nationalist feeling.
items.markingKey: Only this statement matches the content of Source C. [1]

items.stem: Ravi ends an essay on “‘Hitler followed a planned programme of expansion.’ How far do you agree?” with this conclusion: “Hitler had consistent long-term aims but was an opportunist in their timing and method.” Explain one piece of evidence that supports this conclusion and one point a critic could make against it.
items.answer: Evidence the conclusion rests on (either strand of the judgement), for example: Mein Kampf set out the aim of Lebensraum. / He exploited opportunities such as the Anschluss crisis. Possible criticism: the conclusion may underplay the point that the Hossbach Memorandum showed plans for expansion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for relevant supporting evidence and 1 mark for explaining how it supports the judgement; 1 mark for a valid counter-point and 1 mark for developing it [2]

items.stem: Study Source B. Source B: a historian writing in 2000 (illustrative). “The new states inherited borders drawn by colonial officials and populations divided by language, religion and race. The Cold War made these problems more dangerous, but it did not create them.” Assess the reliability of Source B as evidence about nation-building.
items.answer: Reliable because it is a considered interpretation. Less reliable because it is one view. Cross-reference: It does not discuss particular countries. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view, but it needs to be tested against other evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point about the content; up to 2 marks for using the provenance (author, date, purpose, audience) to judge reliability; up to 2 marks for cross-referencing with own knowledge; 1 mark for a supported overall judgement [4]

items.stem: Elena ends an essay on “‘The oil crises were the main cause of stagflation in the 1970s.’ How far do you agree?” with this conclusion: “The oil shocks made stagflation severe, but its roots lay in the spending of the 1960s and declining competitiveness.” Explain one piece of evidence that supports this conclusion and one point a critic could make against it.
items.answer: Evidence the conclusion rests on (either strand of the judgement), for example: Oil prices quadrupled in 1973-74 and rose again in 1979. / Inflation was already rising in the late 1960s because of Vietnam spending. Possible criticism: the conclusion may underplay the point that Each shock was followed by recession.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for relevant supporting evidence and 1 mark for explaining how it supports the judgement; 1 mark for a valid counter-point and 1 mark for developing it [3]

items.stem: ‘Watergate permanently weakened the American presidency.’ Discuss.
items.answer: For: Congress passed the War Powers Act and the Budget and Impoundment Control Act. Public trust in government fell sharply. Ford and Carter were weak presidents. Against: Reagan restored presidential authority in the 1980s. Presidents continued to use military force without declarations. The system showed it could correct abuse. Judgement: Watergate weakened the presidency in the 1970s, but the effect was not permanent, as Reagan showed.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): a focused, balanced and analytical answer with a sustained, well-supported judgement; precise and relevant knowledge throughout. Level 4 (13-16): analysis of both sides with a judgement, though not fully sustained or supported. Level 3 (9-12): some analysis, but one-sided or uneven, or with descriptive passages. Level 2 (5-8): mainly descriptive or narrative, with limited links to the question. Level 1 (1-4): general, unsupported or irrelevant points. (The examination essay is marked out of 30; levels are scaled.) Agree / supporting: Congress passed the War Powers Act and the Budget and Impoundment Control Act. Public trust in government fell sharply. Ford and Carter were weak presidents. Disagree / other factors: Reagan restored presidential authority in the 1980s. Presidents continued to use military force without declarations. The system showed it could correct abuse. Possible judgement: Watergate weakened the presidency in the 1970s, but the effect was not permanent, as Reagan showed. [19]

items.stem: Study Source A. Source A: a confession by a defendant at a Moscow show trial, 1938 (summary). The defendant confessed to plotting with foreign intelligence services to murder Soviet leaders and restore capitalism. Does Source A support the view that the Great Terror was directed mainly by Stalin himself? Explain your answer using the source and your own knowledge.
items.answer: Supports: it shows the regime staging trials directed from the top However, confessions were extracted by torture and threats, so they are not reliable evidence of guilt.

items.stem: Study Source C. Source C: a speech by Mussolini, October 1935 (summary). Announcing the war against Abyssinia, Mussolini told Italians that their country had been denied its place in the sun and that its patience was at an end. Does Source C support the view that Mussolini's foreign policy was driven mainly by a desire for prestige? Explain your answer using the source and your own knowledge.
items.answer: Supports: it stresses national prestige and status However, it is propaganda that may hide other motives.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid judgement; up to 2 marks for details of the source used to support it; up to 2 marks for evaluating the source (provenance or own knowledge) [4]

items.stem: The following extract is from a historian writing in 1992 (illustrative). “American officials did not expect a Soviet attack. What they feared was that the USSR might gain control of the industrial and human resources of Europe and Asia through economic collapse and local communist parties. To prevent this, they sought a preponderance of power, a defensive aim pursued by expansive means.” What can you learn from this extract about the interpretation and approach of the historian who wrote it? Use the extract and your knowledge of the origins of the Cold War to explain your answer.
items.answer: Interpretation: The USA pursued a preponderance of power for defensive reasons, which helped to create the Cold War. Approach: The historian examines US national security policy and how officials perceived threats. Own knowledge that supports it: US officials did not expect an immediate Soviet attack. The Marshall Plan aimed to stabilise Western Europe. NATO and West Germany strengthened the Western position. Own knowledge that challenges it: Soviet actions gave real grounds for fear. Post-Cold War evidence emphasises Stalin's aims. Revisionists see economic motives as more aggressive.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): demonstrates a full understanding of the historian's interpretation and approach, explained with close reference to the extract and tested against accurate own knowledge. Level 4 (13-16): explains the main interpretation with support from the extract and shows some understanding of the approach. Level 3 (9-12): identifies the main interpretation with some support, or explains sub-messages. Level 2 (5-8): identifies sub-messages or makes valid points about the topic linked to the extract. Level 1 (1-4): paraphrases or summarises the extract, or writes about the topic without reference to it. (The examination question is marked out of 40; levels are scaled.) [19]
